parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, genus, species”).

parole.significato: Close, near.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλησίον (plēsíon, “near”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Plutonian (“of or relating to Pluto, the Greek and Roman god of the underworld; demonic, infernal”).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn, “Pluto, Greek and Roman god of the underworld”) (from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “riches, wealth”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to fly; to flow; to run”)) + -ων (-ōn)) + -ic (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). The English word is co

parole.significato: Relating to the lungs.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”).

parole.significato: Relating to a foot or a footlike part.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πούς (poús).

parole.significato: many
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many, much”), from Proto-Indo-European *polh₁ús (“much, many”). Unrelated to -poly.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an insect (especially a bee) which collects pollen from the flowers of a variety of unrelated plants.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “a lot of, much”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *polh₁ús (“many, much”), from the root *pleh₁- (“to fill”)) + λέγειν (légein), from λέγω (légō, “to arrange, choose, gather; to count, reckon”) (from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to gather”)) + -ic.

parole.significato: earlier; prior
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”).

parole.significato: Déjà vu, a sense of having experienced some event before due to an imagined memory.
parole.testo: Coined by philologist and psychical researcher Frederic W. H. Myers (1843-1901) from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “pre-, before”) + μνήμη (mnḗmē, “memory”) + -ία (-ía) on the model of amnesia, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think, mind”). Compare Greek προμνησία (promnisía).

parole.significato: Placed before, added.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “I add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “I place”), from Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti + *dʰédʰeh₁ti (“to be putting, to be placing”).

parole.significato: Placed before, added, at the front, at the tip, before.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “I add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “I place”), from Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti + *dʰédʰeh₁ti (“to be putting, to be placing”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -o-.

parole.significato: The preparation and preliminary oblation of the Eucharistic bread and wine in the Divine Liturgy of the Eastern Orthodo…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρόθεσις (próthesis, “a preposing”), from προτίθημι (protíthēmi, “to prepose”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to place”), from Proto-Indo-European *pro- + *dʰédʰeh₁ti (“to be putting, to be placing”).

parole.significato: pyelonephritis
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πυέλος (puélos, “oblong trough”) + -itis, from Proto-Indo-European *plu- (zero-grade form of *plew-) + *-elos. By surface analysis, pyel- + -itis.

parole.significato: A fruit which, when mature, splits open to release its seeds; a dehiscent fruit.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ῥῆγμα (rhêgma, “something broken or rent asunder; a breach, cleft, fracture”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”)) + English -carp (suffix meaning ‘part of a fruit or fruiting body’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kerp- (“to harvest; to pluck”

parole.significato: An electrical resistor with two terminals, the resistance of which can be varied continuously by moving a knob or slide…
parole.testo: From rheo- (prefix meaning ‘current; flow’) + -stat (suffix forming the names of scientific instruments which render the prefixed elements static or stationary in some respect), coined by the English physicist and inventor Charles Wheatstone (1802–1875) in an 1843 journal article: see the quotation.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a rheme.
parole.testo: Via Ancient Greek ῥῆμα (rhêma, “rheme”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁-.

parole.significato: roots (of living organisms).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ῥῐ́ζᾰ (rhĭ́ză, “root”), from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds.

parole.significato: Solid, three-dimensional.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek στερεο- (stereo-), combining form of στερεός (stereós, “firm, solid”).

parole.significato: Natural affection or love, especially of parents for their children.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek στοργή (storgḗ, “affection, love (especially of parents and children)”), from στέργω (stérgō, “to love (chiefly of non-sexual affection); to show affection”) (from Proto-Indo-European *sterg- (“to cover; to protect”)) + -η (-ē, suffix forming action nouns).

parole.significato: fast
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τᾰχῠ́ς (tăkhŭ́s, “swift”).

parole.significato: A fictional creature, resembling a centaur, with the lower body of some four-or-more-legged animal and an upper body ei…
parole.testo: Clipping of centaur, corresponding to Ancient Greek ταῦρος (taûros, “bull”), from Proto-Indo-European *táwros. Doublet of steer.

parole.significato: over a distance
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “at a distance, far off, far away, far from”).

parole.significato: a grossly malformed fetus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τέρας (téras).

parole.significato: An undifferentiated plant body, such as in algae.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós, “young shoot, twig”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelh₁- (“to bloom”).

parole.significato: containing sulfur, especially a compound in which oxygen has been replaced by this element
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek θεῖον (theîon, “sulfur”).

parole.significato: sections; cutting
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “section, slice”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *temh₁- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: The art of making relief or intaglio designs, especially by chasing, carving or embossing in metal
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τορευτικός (toreutikós, “of metal work”), from τορευτός (toreutós, “worked in relief”), from τορέω (toréō, “I work in relief”), from τορευς (toreus, “a boring tool”), from Proto-Indo-European *terə-.

parole.significato: friction
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τρίβω (tríbō, “to rub”).

parole.significato: urine; relating to urine and the urinary system.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οὖρον (oûron).

parole.significato: A type of long thrusting lance, used in ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ξυστόν (xustón, “spear, javelin”), of unknown origin. Potentially from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰasto- or *ǵʰasdʰo- (“branch ~ spear, sharp spine”) (whence also gad, goad, and yard), but this is likely a substrate word in view of the various irregularities.

parole.significato: A eukaryotic cell formed from the fusion of two gametes (“reproductive cells”) during a fertilization process.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ζῠγωτός (zŭgōtós, “yoked”) + English -ote (suffix meaning ‘having [the thing to which it is attached]’). parole.significato: A ferment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζύμη (zúmē, “leaven”).
